messages.subject: bifactor model with binary variables
parts:
Hello!

I tried to fit a bifactor model, which contains one general factor and two specific factors, based on 18 binary variables (N=259). 

here's the code:

model<- '
general =~ Q1a + Q2a + Q3a + Q4a + Q5a + Q6a + Q7a + Q8a + Q9a + Q10a + Q11a + Q12a + Q13a + Q14a + Q15a + Q16a + Q17a + Q18a
att =~ Q1a + Q2a + Q3a + Q4a + Q5a + Q6a + Q7a + Q8a + Q9a
hyp =~ Q10a + Q11a + Q12a + Q13a + Q14a + Q15a + Q16a + Q17a + Q18a
'
fit<- cfa (model, data=data, estimator="WLSMV", orthogonal=TRUE, ordered=c("Q1a", "Q2a", "Q3a", "Q4a", "Q5a", "Q6a", "Q7a", "Q8a", "Q9a", "Q10a", "Q11a", "Q12a", "Q13a", "Q14a", "Q15a", "Q16a", "Q17a", "Q18a"))
summary(fit, fit.measures=TRUE, standardized=TRUE)

I get this warning massages:

Warning messages:
1: In lavaan::lavaan(model = two.model, data = datar, meanstructure = TRUE,  :
  lavaan WARNING: some estimated variances are negative
2: In lavaan::lavaan(model = two.model, data = datar, meanstructure = TRUE,  :
  lavaan WARNING: covariance matrix of latent variables is not positive definite; use inspect(fit,"cov.lv") to investigate.

When I run the same model, but without the ordered=c() part - it manages to run. What could be the problem?

Thanks in advance :)

messages.author: 3fe90052fbf2f899
messages.subject: Re: bifactor model with binary variables
parts:
I get this warning massages:

Warning messages:
1: In lavaan::lavaan(model = two.model, data = datar, meanstructure = TRUE,  :
  lavaan WARNING: some estimated variances are negative
2: In lavaan::lavaan(model = two.model, data = datar, meanstructure = TRUE,  :
  lavaan WARNING: covariance matrix of latent variables is not positive definite; use inspect(fit,"cov.lv") to investigate.
As the messages indicate, you have a Heywood case (negative variance estimate), and you can use the inspect() function to find out which parameter it is.
When I run the same model, but without the ordered=c() part - it manages to run. What could be the problem?

Well, there's no reason to expect that fitting the model to different data (ordered vs. continuous) will yield the same results.  They can yield similar results under certain circumstances:

http://dx.doi.org/10.1037/a0029315

But you can get Heywood cases regardless of the estimator, and they can indicate either model misspecification, or perhaps just sampling error if you fit a model in which the population values happen to be close to a natural boundary.  This paper talks about testing the null hypothesis of the sampling-error explanation (but it is still worth considering whether your model is misspecified by looking at fit measures and standardized residuals):

http://dx.doi.org/10.1177/0049124112442138

Terry
